sections.name: Security Architecture & Zero Trust Design
sections.explanation_simple: Security architecture is designing the overall security of a system or organization from the ground up. Instead of adding security after problems appear (which never works well), good security architecture builds protection into the foundation. Zero Trust is the modern approach: 'never trust, always verify'. In the old model, if you were inside the corporate network, you were trusted. Zero Trust says: every request, from anywhere, must be verified. This means micro-segmentation (every part of the network is isolated), least privilege (minimum access), continuous verification (always checking), and assume breach (design assuming an attacker is already inside).
key_concepts: Zero Trust: Never trust, always verify - no implicit trust based on network location
Micro-Segmentation: Dividing networks into small isolated zones (even between servers)
Defense in Depth: Multiple layers of security (firewall + EDR + MFA + encryption + monitoring)
Assume Breach: Design your security assuming an attacker is already inside your network
Network Segmentation: Separating different security zones (public, private, sensitive, DMZ)
DMZ: Demilitarized Zone - public-facing servers isolated from internal network
Security by Design: Security requirements built into system design from day one
Privacy by Design: Privacy considerations built into system design (GDPR requirement)
Threat Modeling: Identifying potential threats during system design (before implementation)
Crown Jewels: The most valuable assets you're protecting (customer data, source code, keys)
Trust Zones: Areas of different trust levels (untrusted: internet, low trust: DMZ, high trust: internal)
Just-in-Time Access: Privileges granted only when needed, for limited time
PIM/PAM: Privileged Identity/Access Management - securing admin accounts
CASB: Cloud Access Security Broker - security between users and cloud services
SASE: Secure Access Service Edge - network + security in a converged cloud service
ZTNA: Zero Trust Network Access - replacing VPNs with zero trust remote access

code_examples.title: Zero Trust Architecture Design Pattern
code_examples.code:
# ===== ZERO TRUST ARCHITECTURE DESIGN =====

"""
ZERO TRUST COMPONENTS:

                    Internet
                       |
            +----------+----------+
            |          |          |
         WAF/API   Email      External
         Gateway    Gateway    Apps
            |          |          |
            +----------+----------+
                       |
                +------+------+
                |  Identity  |
                |  Provider  |
                +------+------+
                       |
            +----------+----------+
            |          |          |
      +-----+---+  +--+-----+  +-+--------+
      |         |  |        |  |          |
   Dev/User  Service   Data    Admin
   (Verified) (mTLS)  (Encrypt) (JIT)
      |         |        |        |
      +----+----+--------+--------+
           |
      +----+----+
      |  SIEM/  |
      |  SOAR   |
      +---------+


IMPLEMENTATION CHECKLIST:

[ ] 1. IDENTITY AS THE NEW PERIMETER
    - All access requires authentication (no network-level trust)
    - MFA for ALL users (including service accounts)
    - Continuous authentication (not just at login)

[ ] 2. DEVICE TRUST
    - Devices must be compliant before accessing resources
    - Endpoint detection (EDR) required on all devices
    - Certificate-based device identity

[ ] 3. MICRO-SEGMENTATION
    - Every workload has its own security group
    - East-West traffic (between servers) is also inspected
    - No flat networks anywhere

[ ] 4. LEAST PRIVILEGE ACCESS
    - Just-in-Time (JIT) admin access
    - Just-Enough-Access (JEA) - minimum permissions
    - Regular access reviews and certification

[ ] 5. ENCRYPT EVERYTHING
    - All data encrypted at rest (AES-256)
    - All data encrypted in transit (TLS 1.3)
    - mTLS between all services (mutual TLS)

[ ] 6. CONTINUOUS MONITORING
    - 100% logging (no missing data)
    - Automated threat detection (UEBA, ML)
    - Automated incident response

[ ] 7. ASSUME BREACH
    - Have rollback plans
    - Practice incident response regularly
    - Honey tokens (fake credentials to detect attackers)
"""

# Python: Network segmentation validator (simplified)
from ipaddress import IPv4Network, IPv4Address

class NetworkSegmentation:
    def __init__(self):
        self.zones = {
            'public': IPv4Network('203.0.113.0/24'),
            'dmz': IPv4Network('10.0.1.0/24'),
            'internal': IPv4Network('10.0.2.0/24'),
            'sensitive': IPv4Network('10.0.3.0/24'),
            'admin': IPv4Network('10.0.99.0/24'),
        }

        # Allowed traffic between zones
        self.rules = [
            ('internet', 'public', ['80', '443']),
            ('internet', 'dmz', ['443']),
            ('dmz', 'internal', ['80', '443', '3306']),
            ('internal', 'sensitive', ['443', '1433']),
            ('admin', 'internal', ['22', '3389', '443']),
            ('admin', 'sensitive', ['22', '443']),
        ]

    def validate_traffic(self, source_ip, dest_ip, port):
        """Check if traffic between two IPs is allowed."""
        source_zone = self._identify_zone(source_ip)
        dest_zone = self._identify_zone(dest_ip)

        if not source_zone or not dest_zone:
            return False, "Unknown zone"

        for src, dst, ports in self.rules:
            if src == source_zone and dst == dest_zone:
                if port in ports:
                    return True, "Allowed by policy"

        return False, f"No rule allows {source_zone} -> {dest_zone} on port {port}"

    def _identify_zone(self, ip):
        ip = IPv4Address(ip)
        for name, network in self.zones.items():
            if ip in network:
                return name
        return None

sections.name: Compliance & Legal Frameworks
sections.explanation_simple: Compliance frameworks are sets of security requirements that companies must follow. If you handle credit cards, you must follow PCI DSS. If you handle European user data, you must follow GDPR. If you're a healthcare provider in the US, HIPAA applies. If you're a service provider, SOC 2 might be required. These frameworks tell you exactly what security controls you need to have in place. They're not optional - they're legal requirements with serious fines for non-compliance. Understanding them is essential for any security professional because they drive what companies actually invest in security-wise.
key_concepts: GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation): EU data privacy law - applies to ANY company with EU users
GDPR Fines: Up to 4% of global revenue or 20M euros (whichever is higher)
SOC 2: Service Organization Control 2 - audit for service providers (security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy)
ISO 27001: International standard for Information Security Management Systems (ISMS)
PCI DSS: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (if you handle credit cards)
HIPAA: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (US healthcare data)
SOX: Sarbanes-Oxley Act (financial reporting controls for public companies)
NIST CSF: National Institute of Standards and Technology Cybersecurity Framework
CIS Controls: Center for Internet Security's 18 critical security controls
FedRAMP: US Government cloud security standard
DPIA: Data Protection Impact Assessment (GDPR requirement for high-risk processing)
DPO: Data Protection Officer (required for some organizations under GDPR)
Data Processor vs Controller: Who collects data vs who processes it on behalf
Breach Notification: GDPR requires notification within 72 hours
Right to Erasure: 'Right to be forgotten' - users can request data deletion
Data Portability: Users can request their data in a machine-readable format

code_examples.code:
# ===== GDPR COMPLIANCE CHECKLIST =====

"""
=== DATA MAPPING ===
[ ] Inventory of all personal data collected
[ ] Data flow diagrams (where data goes, who processes it)
[ ] Data retention schedule (how long you keep each type)
[ ] Data Processing Agreement (DPA) with all vendors

=== LAWFUL BASIS ===
[ ] Document lawful basis for each processing activity
[ ] Consent: opt-in, specific, informed, withdrawable
[ ] Legitimate Interest Assessment (LIA) if using legitimate interest
[ ] Contract necessity (data needed to deliver service)

=== DATA SUBJECT RIGHTS ===
[ ] Right to be informed (privacy notice on all data collection points)
[ ] Right of access (DSAR - Data Subject Access Request process)
[ ] Right to rectification (correct inaccurate data)
[ ] Right to erasure (delete data on request)
[ ] Right to restrict processing
[ ] Right to data portability
[ ] Right to object (marketing, profiling)
[ ] Rights related to automated decision-making

=== TECHNICAL MEASURES ===
[ ] Encryption at rest (AES-256 for personal data)
[ ] Encryption in transit (TLS 1.3)
[ ] Access controls (least privilege)
[ ] Pseudonymization where possible
[ ] Backup and disaster recovery
[ ] Incident response plan

=== ORGANIZATIONAL MEASURES ===
[ ] Data Protection Officer (DPO) appointed
[ ] Staff training on data protection
[ ] Breach notification procedure (72 hours!)
[ ] Vendor due diligence process
[ ] Regular security assessments

=== FOR ENGINEERS (Technical Implementation) ===
"""

# 1. Data encryption implementation
from cryptography.fernet import Fernet
import hashlib

def encrypt_pii(data: str, key: bytes) -> bytes:
    """Encrypt personal data at rest."""
    f = Fernet(key)
    return f.encrypt(data.encode())

def decrypt_pii(encrypted_data: bytes, key: bytes) -> str:
    """Decrypt personal data."""
    f = Fernet(key)
    return f.decrypt(encrypted_data).decode()

def pseudonymize(data: str) -> str:
    """Pseudonymize: replace identifier with a hash."""
    return hashlib.sha256(data.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]

# 2. Data deletion (Right to Erasure)
def delete_user_data(user_id: str, database):
    """Delete all personal data for a user."""
    tables = ['users', 'profiles', 'payment_info', 'activity_logs', 'preferences']
    for table in tables:
        database.execute(f"DELETE FROM {table} WHERE user_id = ?", (user_id,))
    # Also check: backups (mark for deletion), cached data, logs
    print(f"All personal data deleted for user {user_id}")

# 3. Data portability (Right to Data Portability)
def export_user_data(user_id: str, database) -> dict:
    """Export all user data in machine-readable format (JSON)."""
    user_data = {}
    tables = ['profiles', 'preferences', 'activity_logs']
    for table in tables:
        rows = database.execute(f"SELECT * FROM {table} WHERE user_id = ?", (user_id,)).fetchall()
        user_data[table] = [dict(row) for row in rows]
    return user_data  # Return as JSON response

# Python: Compliance gap analysis tool
class ComplianceGapAnalysis:
    def __init__(self, framework_name, required_controls):
        self.framework = framework_name
        self.required = required_controls
        self.implemented = []
        self.partial = []
        self.missing = []

    def assess(self, current_controls):
        """Assess current implementation against required controls."""
        for control in self.required:
            status = current_controls.get(control, {}).get('status', 'Not Implemented')
            if status == 'Implemented':
                self.implemented.append(control)
            elif status in ['In Progress', 'Partial']:
                self.partial.append(control)
            else:
                self.missing.append(control)

    def generate_report(self):
        """Generate compliance gap report."""
        total = len(self.required)
        print(f"=== {self.framework} COMPLIANCE GAP ANALYSIS ===")
        print(f"Total controls: {total}")
        print(f"Implemented: {len(self.implemented)} ({len(self.implemented)/total*100:.0f}%)")
        print(f"Partial: {len(self.partial)} ({len(self.partial)/total*100:.0f}%)")
        print(f"Missing: {len(self.missing)} ({len(self.missing)/total*100:.0f}%)")
        print()
        if self.missing:
            print("CRITICAL GAPS (must address immediately):")
            for ctrl in self.missing[:5]:
                print(f"  - {ctrl}: {self.required[ctrl]['title']}")
            print(f"  ... and {len(self.missing)-5} more")
        return len(self.missing) == 0

sections.name: Pentest Reporting & Communication
sections.explanation_simple: Pentest reporting is the most underestimated skill in cybersecurity. The best hacker in the world is useless if they can't communicate their findings to the people who need to fix them. A great pentest report has two versions: an executive summary (1-2 pages for non-technical managers - no jargon, just risks and business impact) and a technical report (detailed findings with reproduction steps, screenshots, and remediation guidance). The most important part is the risk rating - you need to clearly communicate which vulnerabilities are critical (fix now) vs informational (nice to fix).
key_concepts: Executive Summary: 1 page for management - no technical jargon, focus on business risk
Technical Report: Full details for developers/IT - reproduction steps, proof of concept, remediation
Risk Rating: CVSS scoring or custom rating (Critical/High/Medium/Low/Info)
CVSS: Common Vulnerability Scoring System (0-10 scale, uses vector string)
Finding: A single vulnerability with full details (typically 0.5-2 pages per finding)
Proof of Concept (PoC): Actually showing the vulnerability works (screenshot, video, code)
Remediation: Clear instructions on how to fix each finding
False Positive: A reported vulnerability that doesn't actually exist (wastes everyone's time)
Scope Creep: Testing things that weren't agreed upon (could get you in legal trouble)
Rules of Engagement: The contract defining what, when, and how you'll test

code_examples.title: Professional Pentest Report Template
code_examples.code:
# ===== PENETRATION TEST REPORT STRUCTURE =====

"""

--- EXECUTIVE SUMMARY (for the CISO/CEO) ---

[COMPANY NAME] Penetration Test Report
[Date]

OVERVIEW
[Company] engaged [Your Company] to perform a penetration test
of [scope] from [date] to [date]. The test simulated a [level]
attacker against [systems].

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
During the assessment, X findings were identified:
- Critical: X
- High: X
- Medium: X
- Low: X

The most significant finding was [highest severity finding],
which could allow an attacker to [impact].

We recommend prioritizing the remediation of the critical and
high findings within [timeframe].

KEY FINDINGS (Management View):
1. [Finding name]: [1 sentence impact] - CRITICAL
2. [Finding name]: [1 sentence impact] - HIGH
3. [Finding name]: [1 sentence impact] - HIGH

POSITIVES:
- [Good things we found - well configured system X, etc.]
- [Security control Y worked as expected]


--- TECHNICAL REPORT (for developers/IT) ---

1. FINDING: SQL Injection in User Search
   Severity: Critical (CVSS 9.8)
   Location: GET /api/users/search?q=*
   CWE: CWE-89
   
   Description:
   The user search endpoint does not sanitize input before
   including it in a SQL query. An attacker can extract
   the entire database, including password hashes and PII.
   
   Steps to Reproduce:
   1. Navigate to /api/users/search?q=test
   2. Capture request in Burp Suite
   3. Modify q parameter to: ' UNION SELECT * FROM users--
   4. Observe that all user records are returned
   
   Proof of Concept:
   curl -X GET "https://app.example.com/api/users/search?q=' UNION SELECT * FROM users--"
   
   Impact:
   - Complete database disclosure (users, payment info)
   - Potential account takeover
   - Data breach reporting requirements
   
   Remediation:
   Use parameterized queries:
   
   // VULNERABLE:
   $query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name LIKE '%" . $_GET['q'] . "%'";
   
   // SECURE:
   $stmt = $pdo->prepare("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name LIKE ?");
   $stmt->execute(['%' . $_GET['q'] . '%']);
   
   Additionally, implement:
   - Input validation (reject special characters)
   - WAF rule to block SQL injection patterns
   - Least privilege database account
   
   References:
   - OWASP SQL Injection: https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/SQL_Injection

2. FINDING: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) in Profile Name
   Severity: Medium (CVSS 6.1)
   ...


--- APPENDIX ---

A. SCOPE
   In-scope:
   - app.example.com (production)
   - api.example.com (production)
   
   Out-of-scope:
   - Any third-party services
   - Physical security
   - Social engineering

B. TOOLS USED
   - Burp Suite Professional
   - Nmap, RustScan
   - Nuclei
   - Custom Python scripts
   - SQLMap

C. METHODOLOGY
   - OWASP Testing Guide v4
   - PTES (Penetration Testing Execution Standard)

D. RETEST RESULTS
   (To be filled after remediation verification)

E. GLOSSARY
   - CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures
   - CVSS: Common Vulnerability Scoring System
   - CWE: Common Weakness Enumeration
"""

sections.name: Secure Development Lifecycle (SDLC) & DevSecOps
sections.explanation_simple: Secure Development Lifecycle (SDLC) means building security into every phase of software development, not checking for bugs at the end. The old way: write code -> test features -> release -> find security bugs -> panic. The DevSecOps way: train developers -> design with threat modeling -> write code with security reviews -> auto-scan for vulnerabilities in CI/CD -> test in staging -> monitor in production. The key principle is 'shift left' - find and fix security issues as early as possible (it's 100x cheaper to fix during design than after release).
key_concepts: Shift Left: Finding security issues earlier in development (cheaper to fix)
SAST (Static Application Security Testing): Scanning source code for vulnerabilities (white-box, before running)
DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing): Testing running applications (black-box, like a hacker)
IAST (Interactive Application Security Testing): Instrumented testing that sees inside the running app
RASP (Runtime Application Self-Protection): Security built into the running application
SCA (Software Composition Analysis): Scanning dependencies for known vulnerabilities (npm audit, pip-audit, Dependabot)
Threat Modeling STRIDE: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, DoS, Elevation of Privilege
DREAD: Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected Users, Discoverability (risk rating model)
CI/CD Security: Security integrated into build pipeline (auto-scan on every commit)
Pre-commit Hooks: Security checks before code is committed (prevent secrets from reaching repo)
Secret Scanning: Detecting API keys, passwords, tokens committed to source code (git-secrets, truffleHog)
Dependency Scanning: Checking third-party libraries for known CVEs (OWASP Dependency-Check, Snyk)
Container Scanning: Scanning Docker images for vulnerabilities (Trivy, Clair)
SBOM: Software Bill of Materials - inventory of all components and dependencies
Security Champions: Developers trained in security who advocate for secure practices in their teams

code_examples.title: DevSecOps Pipeline (GitHub Actions)
code_examples.code:
# ===== DEVSECOPS CI/CD PIPELINE =====
# .github/workflows/security.yml

name: Security Scan

on:
  push:
    branches: [main, develop]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 6 * * 1'  # Weekly scan on Monday

jobs:
  security:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      # 1. SECRETS SCANNING (check for committed secrets)
      - name: Secrets Scanning
        uses: trufflesecurity/trufflehog@v3
        with:
          extra_args: --results=verified,unknown

      # 2. SAST - Static Analysis
      - name: SAST with Semgrep
        uses: semgrep/semgrep-action@v1
        with:
          config: p/default  # OWASP Top 10, CWE Top 25

      # 3. DEPENDENCY SCANNING
      - name: Dependency Review
        uses: actions/dependency-review-action@v3
        with:
          fail-on-severity: high

      - name: SCA with Trivy
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
        with:
          scan-type: fs
          scan-ref: .
          format: sarif
          output: trivy-results.sarif
          severity: CRITICAL,HIGH

      # 4. CONTAINER SCANNING (if building Docker images)
      - name: Build and Scan Container
        if: github.event_name == 'push'
        run: |
          docker build -t myapp:${{ github.sha }} .
          trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH myapp:${{ github.sha }}

      # 5. SECRETS IN CODE (another layer)
      - name: GitLeaks
        uses: gitleaks/gitleaks-action@v2

      # 6. UPLOAD RESULTS
      - name: Upload SARIF to GitHub
        if: always()
        uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v2
        with:
          sarif_file: trivy-results.sarif

      # 7. BLOCK ON CRITICAL FINDINGS
      - name: Check for Critical Vulnerabilities
        if: failure()
        run: |
          echo "::error::Critical vulnerabilities found! Fix before merging."
          exit 1


# ===== PRE-COMMIT HOOKS (gitleaks + secrets detection) =====
# .pre-commit-config.yaml

repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
    rev: v8.16.1
    hooks:
      - id: gitleaks
  - repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks
    rev: v4.4.0
    hooks:
      - id: detect-aws-credentials
      - id: detect-private-key
  - repo: https://github.com/PyCQA/bandit
    rev: 1.7.5
    hooks:
      - id: bandit
        args: ["-ll"]

# Install: pre-commit install
# Now every commit is scanned!


# ===== THREAT MODELING WITH STRIDE =====
"""
THREAT MODELING TEMPLATE:

System: User Authentication Service

| # | Threat | STRIDE | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|--------|--------|--------|------------|
| 1 | Attacker spoofs another user's identity | S | Account takeover | MFA required, strong password policy |
| 2 | Attacker tampers with JWT token | T | Access other user data | JWT signature verification, short expiry |
| 3 | User denies performing an action | R | Non-repudiation fails | Audit logging all auth events |
| 4 | Password database leaked | I | Credential theft | bcrypt/argon2 hashing, no plaintext storage |
| 5 | Login endpoint DoS | D | Service unavailable | Rate limiting, WAF, auto-scaling |
| 6 | SQL injection in login | E | Database compromise | Parameterized queries, input validation |

PASTA: Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis
  - More detailed than STRIDE
  - 7 stages: Define objectives -> Define technical scope -> App decomposition -> Threat analysis -> Vulnerability analysis -> Attack modeling -> Risk and impact analysis
"""

sections.name: Automation & Security Tool Development
sections.explanation_simple: Security automation is about writing tools that do the boring work for you. Instead of manually testing for vulnerabilities, you write scripts that automate the testing. Instead of manually analyzing logs, you write scripts that flag suspicious patterns. Key areas: building custom scanners (for specific vulnerability types), automating recon workflows (finding targets faster), creating assistive security tooling using AI/LLMs, and developing exploit automation. Python is the primary language for security tooling because of its extensive libraries for networking, parsing, and automation.
key_concepts: Custom Vulnerability Scanner: Script that finds specific vulnerability patterns automatically
Web Scraping for Recon: Automated data gathering from public sources
API Wrapper: Programmatic access to security tools (Nmap, Nuclei, Shodan APIs)
Parallel Processing: Speed up scanning by running tasks in parallel (asyncio, multiprocessing)
Result Parsing: Converting tool output (XML, JSON, text) into actionable data
Notification Systems: Alerting via Slack, Discord, email when findings are discovered
Report Generation: Auto-generating security reports from scan results
Playbook Automation: Automating incident response steps (e.g., isolate host on EDR, block IP in firewall)
AI-Assisted Security: Using LLMs to analyze logs, generate detection rules, write reports
SOAR: Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response platforms (automating entire workflows)

code_examples.code:
# ===== CUSTOM VULNERABILITY SCANNER =====
import asyncio
import aiohttp
import json
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List, Optional

@dataclass
class Finding:
    url: str
    vulnerability: str
    severity: str
    description: str
    evidence: str

class CustomScanner:
    def __init__(self, targets: List[str]):
        self.targets = targets
        self.findings: List[Finding] = []

    async def check_security_headers(self, session, url):
        """Check for missing security headers."""
        try:
            async with session.get(url, timeout=10) as response:
                headers = response.headers

                checks = {
                    'Strict-Transport-Security': {
                        'severity': 'Medium',
                        'description': 'Missing HSTS header - no forced HTTPS'
                    },
                    'Content-Security-Policy': {
                        'severity': 'Medium',
                        'description': 'Missing CSP header - vulnerable to XSS'
                    },
                    'X-Content-Type-Options': {
                        'severity': 'Low',
                        'description': 'Missing X-Content-Type-Options header'
                    },
                    'X-Frame-Options': {
                        'severity': 'Medium',
                        'description': 'Missing X-Frame-Options - clickjacking risk'
                    }
                }

                for header, info in checks.items():
                    if header not in headers:
                        self.findings.append(Finding(
                            url=url,
                            vulnerability=f'Missing {header}',
                            severity=info['severity'],
                            description=info['description'],
                            evidence=f'Header {header} is not present in response'
                        ))
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"Error scanning {url}: {e}")

    async def check_cors(self, session, url):
        """Test CORS configuration."""
        try:
            # Test with a malicious origin
            malicious_origin = 'https://evil.com'
            headers = {'Origin': malicious_origin}
            async with session.get(url, headers=headers) as response:
                cors_header = response.headers.get('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', '')
                if cors_header == '*' or malicious_origin in cors_header:
                    self.findings.append(Finding(
                        url=url,
                        vulnerability='Permissive CORS',
                        severity='Medium',
                        description='CORS allows any origin to make cross-origin requests',
                        evidence=f'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: {cors_header}'
                    ))
        except Exception as e:
            pass

    async def check_open_redirect(self, session, url):
        """Test for open redirect vulnerability."""
        try:
            # Basic open redirect test
            payloads = [
                '//evil.com',
                'https://evil.com',
                '/redirect?url=https://evil.com',
                '//evil.com@valid.com'
            ]
            for payload in payloads:
                full_url = f'{url}?next={payload}'
                async with session.get(full_url, allow_redirects=False) as response:
                    location = response.headers.get('Location', '')
                    if 'evil.com' in location:
                        self.findings.append(Finding(
                            url=full_url,
                            vulnerability='Open Redirect',
                            severity='Medium',
                            description='URL redirects to attacker-controlled domain',
                            evidence=f'Redirect to: {location}'
                        ))
                        break
        except Exception as e:
            pass

    async def scan_target(self, target_url):
        """Run all security checks against a target."""
        connector = aiohttp.TCPConnector(limit=10)
        async with aiohttp.ClientSession(connector=connector) as session:
            await asyncio.gather(
                self.check_security_headers(session, target_url),
                self.check_cors(session, target_url),
                self.check_open_redirect(session, target_url),
            )

    async def run(self):
        """Run scanner against all targets."""
        print(f"[*] Scanning {len(self.targets)} targets...")
        await asyncio.gather(*[self.scan_target(url) for url in self.targets])

    def generate_report(self, output_file='findings.json'):
        """Generate JSON report."""
        report = {
            'scan_date': '2024-01-15',
            'total_targets': len(self.targets),
            'total_findings': len(self.findings),
            'findings': [f.__dict__ for f in sorted(
                self.findings,
                key=lambda x: ['Critical', 'High', 'Medium', 'Low'].index(x.severity)
            )]
        }
        with open(output_file, 'w') as f:
            json.dump(report, f, indent=2)
        print(f"[+] Report saved to {output_file}")
        print(f"[+] Total findings: {len(self.findings)}")

# Usage:
# scanner = CustomScanner(["https://example.com"])
# asyncio.run(scanner.run())
# scanner.generate_report()
